name: Gishiri cutting

card.summary: Gishiri cutting is a traditional vaginal-wall incision practised in parts of northern Nigeria and Niger as a remedy for childbirth and fertility concerns, not for appearance; it is documented here for its harms.
card.note: Documented to cause vesicovaginal fistula and other serious injury.

quick.overview:
Gishiri cutting ("salt cut" in Hausa) is a traditional incision into the vaginal wall, performed by traditional practitioners in northern Nigeria and Niger. Practitioners and communities describe it as a remedy for obstructed labour, infertility and related complaints rather than as a cosmetic procedure.

It appears in medical literature mainly as a cause of vesicovaginal fistula, where Nigerian studies have recorded it among the contributing factors.
quick.how: It is described in clinical literature as performed by traditional birth attendants or barbers with a blade. No practice details are given here.
quick.risks: Reported harms include vesicovaginal fistula, urinary incontinence, infection and haemorrhage. One physician's study found over 30 percent of women with such cuts had fistulae.

lead: Gishiri cutting, from the Hausa word for salt, is a traditional procedure in which an incision is made in the vaginal wall, reported in Nigeria and Niger.[1] It is performed in response to infertility, obstructed labour and other conditions, and is not an appearance-related practice.[1]

The World Health Organization's 1995 definition of female genital mutilation included gishiri cuts, but the 2008 definition dropped them because of insufficient information about prevalence and consequences.[1] Nigerian clinical studies have examined its role among causes of vesicovaginal fistula; a study by physician Mairo Usman Mandara found over 30 percent of women with gishiri cuts had fistulae.[1]

Documented injury to bladder and urethra
angle.text: Communities that practise it describe a health or fertility purpose, not a cosmetic one. It is included in the wiki as a documented harmful traditional practice.

paras: The practice is described as an incision of the vaginal wall in response to conditions such as infertility and obstructed labour.[1]

Clinical literature from northern Nigeria identifies gishiri cuts as one cause of vesicovaginal fistula alongside obstructed labour.[1] Mandara's study found fistulae in over 30 percent of women with gishiri cuts.[1]
Nigerian case-control and epidemiological studies of vesicovaginal fistula have examined traditional practices among risk factors, including studies from Maiduguri and northern Nigeria.[2][3]

timeline.event: WHO definition of FGM includes gishiri cutting.[1]
